n: In this lecture we shall consider the topic "Introduction to forensic medicine". The topic has four parts: the science and its tasks, history and the contribution of Uzbekistan, procedural foundations, and organisational structure. Forensic medicine studies medico-biological questions, and its practical form is forensic medical examination. The examination is carried out on the basis of a ruling of the inquiry and investigation bodies or a court order. Learning outcome: the student distinguishes the basic concepts, lists the rights and duties of the expert, and draws the structure of the bureau.

t: The concept of forensic medicine and forensic medical examination
n: The first concept. Forensic medicine is the science that studies the medico-biological questions arising in court, investigation and inquiry. It is a body of knowledge for establishing and evaluating the medical facts that serve as a source of evidence. The scientific and practical investigation carried out by physicians is the application of the science in practice, and it ends with a conclusion. Remember the chain: first a request arrives with a ruling or court order, then the investigation is carried out using medical knowledge, and finally the expert's conclusion is drawn up.

In essence an examination is an investigation, and four features are present together. First, the performer: a specialist with knowledge of his field. Second, the task: a specific task, usually an evaluation. Third, the procedure: it must be strictly defined. Fourth, the document: the result is formalised in a document. The forensic medical expert approaches medical circumstances for the purpose of legal evaluation, whereas the physician does so for treatment. Remember: P–T–P–D, that is, performer, task, procedure, document.

t: Subject and components of forensic medicine
n: The subject of forensic medicine is the theory and practice of examination, that is, the application of special knowledge for judicial and investigative purposes. The system of the subject was first proposed in 1948 by M. I. Avdeev. In 2002 the section on professional offences became a separate discipline, "Legal foundations of medical practice". The main sections are shown in the diagram. Thanatology studies death and changes in the body. Traumatology studies injury, mechanism and circumstances, and toxicology poisons and the diagnosis of poisoning. Obstetrics and gynaecology deal with disputed sexual conditions and offences.

The subject system is linked with Avdeev's proposal. In 1948 M. I. Avdeev first proposed a scientifically substantiated system of the subject of forensic medicine. This system is based on forensic medical practice and closely tied to the objects of examination. The system consists of eight parts: history of development, organisational and procedural questions, external factors and death, inspection and examination of the dead body, and examination of living persons. The remaining parts are physical evidence, investigation and court materials, and examination of professional offences of medical staff.

We turn to the current components of the science. In 1999 V. L. Popov distinguished three main doctrines within the science: death and postmortem changes, injuries, and personal identification. At present the science consists of nine components. These are history, organisational and procedural foundations, thanatology, traumatology, toxicology, obstetrics and gynaecology, forensic medical biology, the effects of various external factors, and the identification of persons and of the injuring instrument. In 2002 the section on professional offences separated into a distinct science, "Legal foundations of medical practice".

t: Links of forensic medicine with other sciences
n: Forensic medicine is not a fundamental but an applied science. It is linked with the medical, legal, natural and philosophical sciences. The medical group includes anatomy, physiology and the clinical sciences. In the legal group there are criminal and civil law and criminalistics. Of the natural sciences, chemistry, physics, biology and mathematics are needed. From philosophy the laws of dialectics and logic are taken. The treating physician approaches for the purpose of treatment, whereas the expert does so for the legal evaluation of circumstances. Pathological anatomy, traumatology, toxicology and obstetrics-gynaecology assist the examination.

Quick question: are forensic medicine as a science and forensic medical examination the same thing? Answer: the science is a body of knowledge, and the examination is the practical application of that knowledge. Recall the features of an examination: it is carried out by a specialist, on a definite task, its procedure is strictly defined, and the result is formalised in a document. Attention: risk of error, science ≠ examination. The science is a system of knowledge, whereas the examination is an investigation that ends with the expert's conclusion. Question for discussion: can an investigation that has been carried out be called an examination if no expert's conclusion is drawn up? Answer relying on the definition.

Principles of forensic medical examination. The law recognises legality, respect for human rights, independence of the expert, objectivity, comprehensiveness and completeness as the main principles. The expert works only within the limits of his competence. Independence gives rise to personal responsibility for the investigation and conclusion. Right of initiative: the expert also expresses an opinion on other questions of importance to the case. Attention: this does not mean collecting material independently. One more point: an object is a source of evidence only during a certain period. Most abrasions and bruises are best examined within the first 10–15 days.

There are four objects of examination. The first is the dead body and its clothing. The second is living persons, that is, the victim and the accused. The third is physical evidence: blood, hair, secretions and stains. The fourth is case materials, for example medical records and protocols. The objects are presented by the person who ordered the examination, who answers for their authenticity. Attention: the expert does not collect the object himself; it is presented by the person who ordered the examination.

Investigative methods are divided into three groups. A method must be scientifically grounded, simple, give a stable result and permit repeated investigation. General scientific methods include observation, description, comparison and measurement, and are used in different sciences. Particular methods, morphological, clinical, radiological and chemical, belong to a specific science. Special methods establish the identity of a person and an instrument, and are used mainly in forensic medical practice. It is advisable that the results obtained be demonstrable and documented. Only methods permitted or recommended by the Chief Bureau of Forensic Medical Examination are used.

t: Tasks and significance of forensic medicine
n: Tasks and significance of forensic medicine. The science answers the medical and biological questions arising in court and investigation when criminal and civil cases are considered. The forensic medical examination service is a specialised branch of the health-care system, and its main task is to carry out forensic medical examinations. On the basis of examination materials, measures should be taken to improve the quality of medical care and to prevent trauma, poisoning and sudden death. The science assists the law-enforcement bodies, and is also of great importance in improving the quality of treatment and preventive work.

Case analysis. Situation: after the examination of a body, the clinical and pathological diagnoses did not agree. Question: how should the forensic medical service act in such a case? Think for 2 minutes in your group. Now the answer. According to the ministry's order, such cases are regularly discussed at a clinico-anatomical conference. The head of the treatment institution is informed in good time of the discrepancy between diagnoses and of shortcomings in medical care.

t: History of forensic medicine: from antiquity to the 16th century
n: We turn to the history of forensic medicine, from antiquity to the 16th century. The laws of Sparta and the Code of Justinian provided for medical examination and the participation of a physician in judicial proceedings. In the table: 9th–8th century BC, Sparta, the laws of Lycurgus noted the need for medical examination. In 44 BC the body of Caesar was examined by the physician Antistius: of 23 wounds, one proved to be the cause of death. In the 6th century, the Code of Justinian placed a physician's conclusion above a witness's testimony. In 1247 in China the "Xi Yuan Lu" was written: it covers examination of the body, injuries, strangulation, drowning and poisons. The "Carolina" laws of 1532 state that the participation of a physician in cases of murder and poisoning is necessary.

t: Formation of forensic medical practice in Europe
n: Let us consider in sequence the formation of forensic medical practice in Europe. In the 13th century in Bologna, the physician Hugh of Lucca gave opinions of a forensic nature before the tribunal. In the 14th century in France, "royal surgeons" were appointed by royal decree, and the first official examination of a body was carried out in Montpellier. Paré's work covers injuries, mechanical asphyxia, carbon monoxide and lightning strike, and gives samples of conclusions, that is, "reports". In 1681 in Zeitz, Schreyer first applied the lung test to the body of a newborn.

Formation of the science: 16th–20th centuries. In the second half of the 16th century, A. Paré's work covers injuries, mechanical asphyxia, carbon monoxide and conditions related to lightning, and gives samples of conclusions. In 1681 Schreyer first applied the lung test in examining the body of a newborn. In Bohn's work it was proposed to call the science "forensic medicine". N. I. Pirogov produced an anatomical atlas for forensic physicians and gave information on gunshot injuries. The year of the atlas differs in the sources: 1846 and 1841. After the Second World War many textbooks were produced: Prokop in Germany, Simpson in England, Popov, Avdeev, Rayskiy and others in the USSR.

Major scientists and schools of the 19th–20th centuries. In the 19th century, Virchow, Rokitansky, Orth and Casper worked in Germany, and von Hofmann in Austria. In France Tardieu, Brouardel and Orfila are known; in Russia Gromov, Pelikan, Minakov and Neiding. In 1846 N. I. Pirogov produced an anatomical atlas for forensic physicians and also gave information on gunshot injuries. After the Second World War textbooks were produced: Prokop in Germany, Simpson in England, Gonzales in the USA. The grouping by country is shown in the diagram.

t: Central Asia: the Sharia period and thinkers
n: The Sharia period and thinkers in Central Asia. Until the beginning of the 20th century in Central Asia, including Uzbekistan, justice was based on the norms of Sharia, and the involvement of medical representatives was not provided for. Nevertheless, in the works of Beruni, Ibn Sina and Ismail Jurjani information is given that relates to forensic medicine or is connected with it. In Ibn Sina's "Canon of Medicine", information is given on postmortem changes of the body, certain types of violent death, poisons and injuries. Attention: risk of error. This information was the result of study not for the administration of justice but for the purpose of giving correct medical help in such cases.

Departments and scientists of Uzbekistan. Scientific research in forensic medicine began in the 1920s, mainly in connection with departments of higher medical schools. I. V. Markovin headed a department from 1928, and in 1930 became the republic's first chief forensic medical expert. Eydlin introduced medico-criminalistic methods, and Shahobiddinov developed the "Rules" on the severity of injuries. Years the departments opened: Turkestan University 1920, Samarkand Medical Institute 1935, Andijan Medical Institute 1959, Tashkent Paediatric Medical Institute 1972, a course at the Tashkent Institute for the Advanced Training of Physicians 1993.

t: Four periods in the development of the service
n: The development of the service has four periods. First period, until the 1920s: the service relied on the Russian system, and in Turkestan official examinations were carried out only sporadically. Second period, until the 1950s: examinations were carried out by department staff, and in 1945 the Republican Office was opened. Third period, 1950–1991: in 1950 the Chief Bureau was established and territorial bureaus appeared. Fourth period, from 1991: an independent service and new normative documents, including the adoption of the Law "On Forensic Examination".

Quick questions on history and periods. First question: in which year was the Chief Bureau of Forensic Medical Examination of the Ministry of Health established? Answer: 1950. Second question: where and when was the first department of forensic medicine opened? Answer: in the medical faculty of Turkestan University, in 1920. Third question: when and on whose initiative was the Republican Office of Forensic Medical Examination opened? Answer: 1945, Prof. I. V. Markovin. Attention: risk of error! 1945, the office, and 1950, the Chief Bureau, are not the same thing. The office was opened first, and the Chief Bureau was established later.

Case analysis, history section. Situation: in Turkestan at the end of the 19th century, forensic medical examination was carried out under the statute of forensic medicine adopted in Russia in 1842. In the first instance, hospital physicians carried out the examination. In a complex case the second instance took part, that is, hospital chiefs, heads of department and district physicians. Question: in an especially complex case, who gave the final conclusion after the conclusion of the second instance? Answer: the third, highest instance, that is, the physicians of the medical council, gave the final conclusion. Practice in Turkestan was based on this procedure.

Legal terms. Law is a system of rules binding on all, guaranteed by the state, regulating social relations. A statute is a normative document establishing generally binding rules, and a code is a systematic collection of the statutes of one field. Forensic medical examination is most often ordered in criminal investigation, so it depends on the norms of the Criminal Code and the Code of Criminal Procedure. Attention: Criminal Code ≠ Code of Criminal Procedure. The first defines offences and measures of punishment, the second the procedure of investigation and trial.

t: Grounds for ordering an examination and Article 173 of the CCP
n: Grounds for ordering an examination. Forensic medical examination is carried out on the basis of a ruling of the inquiry and investigation bodies or an order of the court. According to Article 173 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, an examination is ordered to establish the cause of death and the nature and degree of severity of bodily injury. Also determined are signs of sexual intercourse, pregnancy and abortion; age, if documents are absent or doubtful; physical condition; and the need for treatment of venereal diseases. In Iskandarov's textbook the determination of the mental state of the accused and the victim is also included among the mandatory cases.

The place of examination may be of three kinds. The first is the forensic medical examination bureau, where creating the conditions is the duty of the head of the institution. The second is outside the bureau, where the conditions are provided by the person who ordered the examination. The third is mixed, that is, partly in the bureau and partly outside it. Example: in exhumation the body is opened at the cemetery, while the materials obtained are examined in the bureau's laboratory.

The difference between expert and specialist. The expert establishes the medical fact and gives a conclusion, draws up the expert's conclusion, is examined in court, and does not disclose investigation data. The specialist helps to find and secure evidence, but does not draw up an independent document. He takes part in scene inspection and exhumation, and does not disclose information without permission. The rights, duties and responsibility of a staff expert and a physician-expert are equal in procedural terms. Attention: expert ≠ specialist. A person who was previously a specialist may be an expert in the same case.

Rights of the expert. The expert familiarises himself with the case materials, takes down the necessary information and files a petition for additional materials or objects. With permission he takes part in investigative actions and the court hearing and asks questions relating to the subject of the examination. In the conclusion he may express an opinion on other questions important for the case beyond those put to him; this is the right of initiative. He also has the right to make a statement if his conclusion is interpreted incorrectly, to give a conclusion in his native language with the help of an interpreter, and to appeal against decisions.

t: Duties and responsibility of the expert
n: Duties and responsibility of the expert. The expert must appear when summoned by the inquirer, investigator, prosecutor or court; if there are grounds for recusal he reports this immediately. He examines the objects comprehensively and fully, gives a well-founded and objective conclusion, and ensures the objects are preserved. He does not disclose information, does not collect materials independently, and reports the result only to the body that ordered the examination. Liability is laid down in the Criminal Code: a knowingly false conclusion is punished under Article 238, disclosure of data under 239, and evasion of giving a conclusion under 240.

t: Recusal of the expert and specialist
n: Recusal of the expert and specialist. Recusal is decided only by the person who ordered the examination: in the inquiry within 24 hours, in court at the same sitting. Grounds for recusal: kinship with one of the parties, material or official dependence, status in the case, that is, being a victim, defendant or witness, and also insufficient qualification. Article 76 of the Code of Criminal Procedure: if the expert is a victim, witness or relative, he may decline to take part. Attention: risk of error, a person who was previously a specialist in this case may later be appointed as an expert.

Quick questions on rights and duties. May an expert express an opinion on a question not put to him but important for the case? Yes, this is his right. May an expert collect material for the examination independently? No, this runs contrary to his duties. To whom may the results of the examination be reported? Only to the body or person who ordered the examination. Who can declare a recusal? The expert himself or the parties interested in the case.

Procedural types of examination. A primary examination investigates the object for the first time and is usually carried out by one expert. A commission examination is ordered in a professional offence or an especially complex case, and is carried out by a commission of experts. A complex examination is carried out with experts of different fields when knowledge beyond medicine is needed. An additional examination fills the gaps of the previous conclusion, usually carried out by the previous expert. A repeat examination is ordered if the conclusion is unfounded or doubtful, and is carried out by two or more experts. A repeat examination cannot be entrusted to the original expert, who can only give explanations. Disagreement of the parties alone is not grounds for a repeat examination.

Attention: additional ≠ repeat examination. An additional examination is ordered to fill the deficiencies and gaps of the original conclusion, usually carried out by the previous expert. A repeat examination is ordered when the conclusion is not substantiated or its correctness is doubtful, and the original expert does not take part in the investigation and drawing up of the conclusion. Disagreement of the parties with the previous conclusion is not by itself grounds for a repeat examination; the reasons for disagreement must be stated in the ruling. Commission ≠ complex: in a commission the experts together draw up a general conclusion, whereas in a complex examination other sciences are involved and each expert signs his own part.

The expert's conclusion consists of three parts. The introduction states the date, basis, expert and questions. The research part gives the methods and results. The concluding part gives answers to the questions, that is, the findings. In an investigation on referral an act is drawn up, and its final part is called the "conclusion". The conclusion is not binding in advance on the investigator and the court; if it is rejected, the reason is stated with justification.

t: Examination in preliminary investigation and in court
n: Examination in preliminary investigation and in court proceeds in stages. In investigation the examination is ordered by the investigator's ruling, and the performer is designated by the head of the expert institution. The expert writes the conclusion. In court the expert takes full part in the sitting and participates in examining the circumstances of the case relating to the subject of the examination. The written conclusion is read out at the court sitting, after which the expert may be questioned on it.

t: Foreign experience: objectivity of the expert
n: Foreign experience: objectivity of the expert. In England and Wales the expert's duty is to the court, and his opinion must not be influenced by the person who requested or paid for it. The professional witness states only the medical fact, whereas the expert witness expresses an opinion on these facts. In Russia the expert is an independent procedural person: he cannot depend on the customer and the parties, nor on the body that appointed him. There the conclusion is regarded as one type of evidence.

Case analysis, procedural section. Situation: the body was sent without the inquirer's ruling, only with a written instruction, and the examination was carried out. Which document is drawn up: a conclusion or an act? On a written instruction or referral, an act of forensic medical examination is drawn up: no receipt of rights and duties is taken, and the final part is called the "conclusion". If the first conclusion is unfounded or doubtful, a repeat examination is ordered; it cannot be entrusted to the original expert. Attention: an additional examination fills deficiencies, a repeat examination is ordered when there is doubt. Disagreement of the parties alone is not grounds for a repeat examination.

t: Organisation of the service in Uzbekistan
n: Organisation of the service in Uzbekistan. The service is mainly within the system of the Ministry of Health, and the military are served by the service of the Ministry of Defence. The chain of management is as follows: Ministry of Health, Chief Forensic Medical Bureau, 13 territorial bureaus, then district and city units. The territorial bureau is subordinate to local health authorities in administrative and financial work, and to the Chief Bureau in methodological work. The head of the Chief Bureau, that is, the chief expert of the republic, directs the service in scientific, methodological and organisational terms.

Bureau structure and departments. The composition of the 13 territorial bureaus in Uzbekistan is the same: all the structures defined in the regulations are present in them. In the morphological, forensic histological department, examination of bodies and tissue microscopy are carried out. The forensic medical outpatient clinic carries out examination of living persons. The department of repeat and commission examinations carries out repeat, commission and complex examinations. Forensic chemistry and biology work with poisons and physical evidence. Medical criminalistics studies the mechanism of injury and the instrument. The organisational and methodological department coordinates the bureau's structures, and the territorial bureau directs the district and city units. The bureau is a separate medical organisation: it has its own territory, buildings, equipment and transport.

t: Tasks of the Chief Bureau and independence of the expert
n: Tasks of the Chief Bureau and independence of the expert. The Chief Forensic Medical Expert of the republic directs examination throughout the country in scientific, methodological and organisational terms. Territorial institutions are subordinate to local health authorities in administrative and financial matters, and to the Chief Bureau in matters of examination and methodology. Attention: the head of the bureau may point out deficiencies but cannot cancel a conclusion. Only the expert who gave it is responsible for a conclusion. If the head considers the conclusion incorrect, he asks the supervising prosecutor for permission for a repeat examination. Medical organisations are obliged to assist.

t: Conclusion: main theses and review questions
n: Conclusion and main theses. Forensic medical examination relies on medical knowledge, is carried out in the established procedure and ends with the expert's conclusion. The examination is carried out on the basis of a ruling of the inquiry or investigation bodies, or an order of the court. There are four objects: the dead body, living persons, physical evidence, and materials of criminal and civil cases. Test yourself: can the head of the bureau cancel a conclusion? Who is responsible for a conclusion?
